claims.claim_text: Building arginine from citrulline is energetically expensive: producing each molecule of argininosuccinate requires hydrolyzing adenosine triphosphate (ATP) down to adenosine monophosphate (AMP). By supplementing with arginine directly, the body is spared that cost, leaving more ATP available to provide fuel for cell function.
claims.verbatim:
This process is expensive in terms of energy
since the production of each molecule of argininosuccinate requires hydrolysis
of adenosine triphosphate (ATP) to adenosine monophosphate (AMP), and by


supplementing with arginine, more ATP is available to provide cell function fuel.

claims.claim_text: Arginine is required for complete and efficient cell division and for wound healing. It also facilitates the biological use and excretion of ammonia, supports the immune system, and helps make stored hormones available to the body.
claims.verbatim:
Arginine is required for complete and efficient cell division, wound healing,
facilitating the biological use of and the excretion of ammonia, immune system
support, and the availability of stored hormones.

claims.claim_text: Oral supplementation of arginine is required for the synthesis of nitric oxide (NO). It also reduces blood pressure, increases blood flow through obstructed blood vessels, shortens healing time following trauma, and is particularly useful for bone trauma.
claims.verbatim:
The oral supplementation of
arginine is required for the synthesis of nitric oxide (NO), the reduction of healing
time following trauma, and is particularly useful for bone trauma; it reduces
blood pressure and increases blood flow through obstructed blood vessels.

claims.claim_text: Wallach highlights a surprising dental use of the amino acid arginine: a toothpaste containing 8% arginine gives rapid, effective relief from tooth pain and sensitivity. It works by prompting the formation of a dentin-like material — made of calcium and phosphate — that plugs the microscopic dentin tubules and coats the tooth's surface, sealing off the tiny channels that carry pain signals. It is one of several everyday roles he assigns arginine, alongside wound healing and nitric-oxide production.
claims.verbatim:
Arginine (8%) toothpaste produces rapid and effective relief from dental pain
by producing a dentin-like material that is made up of calcium and phosphate
that is deposited in the dentin tubules and on the surface of dentin.

claims.claim_text: Arginine has a tidy origin story Wallach relays: it was first isolated in 1886 from a lupin seedling by the Swiss chemist Ernst Schultze. Biochemically, the body builds arginine from citrulline using two enzymes — argininosuccinate synthetase (ASS) and argininosuccinate lyase (ASL) — an energy-costly path, which is one reason he favors supplementing arginine directly. And although mainstream science labels it non-essential, Wallach adds arginine to his own list of essential amino acids, because a chronic deficiency drives specific diseases.
claims.verbatim:
Arginine (Arg) was first isolated in 1886 from a lupin seedling by the Swiss
chemist Ernst Schultze and is synthesized from citrulline by the sequential
employment of the cytosolic enzymes argininosuccinate synthetase (ASS) and

argininosuccinate lyase (ASL).

claims.claim_text: Taurine is one of the amino acids Wallach adds to the classic list of essentials, because over the long haul a deficiency drives a specific disease -- macular degeneration. Chemically it is unusual: a sulfonic acid rather than the carboxyl-acid form most biologically occurring acids take, and the body can synthesize it from methionine. Wallach describes taurine as essential to the cardiovascular system, skeletal muscle, the retina, and the central nervous system, where it conjugates bile acids, acts as an antioxidant, stabilizes membranes, and modulates calcium signaling.
claims.verbatim:
Taurine (Ta) has many biological roles including the conjugation of bile acids,
acts as an antioxidant, osmoregulation, membrane stabilization, and modulation
of calcium signaling. Taurine is essential for the functioning of the cardiovascular
system, skeletal muscle, the retina and the central nervous system.

claims.claim_text: Taurine is one of the compounds the body builds from the amino acid methionine. Wallach describes methionine as an intermediate in the biosynthesis of cysteine, carnitine, taurine, lecithin, phosphatidylcholine, and other phospholipids, meaning the body can produce taurine from methionine.
claims.verbatim:
Methionine is an intermediate
in the biosynthesis of cysteine, carnitine, taurine, lecithin, phosphatidylcholine,
and other phospholipids.

claims.claim_text: Taurine is not risk-free at high intakes. Wallach warns that doses of taurine in excess of 2 grams per day have been shown to contribute to the genesis of psoriasis.
claims.verbatim:
Doses of taurine in excess of 2 gm/day have been shown to contribute to the
genesis of psoriasis.

claims.claim_text: Taurine gets its name from the Latin 'Taurus,' meaning bull or ox — fittingly, since it was first isolated from ox bile in 1827 by the German scientists Friedrich Tiedermann and Leopold Gmelin. Wallach counts it among the amino acids worth adding to the classic essentials, noting its unusual chemistry (it is a sulfonic acid rather than the usual carboxylic kind) and its wide roles in the heart, skeletal muscle, retina, and central nervous system.
claims.verbatim:
Taurine is named after the Latin Taurus, which means bull or ox, as it was first
isolated from ox bile in 1827 by the German scientists Friedrich Tiedermann and
Leopold Gmelin.

claims.claim_text: Tryptophan (Trp) is an essential amino acid — the body cannot synthesize it, so it must come from protein in the diet. It is used to build the body's structural enzyme proteins, and it is the biochemical precursor from which the body makes serotonin (a neurotransmitter), which in turn can become melatonin (a sleep hormone); niacin (vitamin B3) is also synthesized from it. Because its absorption from the intestine is reduced by gluten intolerance, lactose intolerance, and fructose malabsorption, a shortfall lowers blood tryptophan and can produce clinical depression.
claims.verbatim:
Tryptophan (Trp) is an essential amino acid encoded in the standard genetic code
as the codon UGG. Only L-tryptophan is used in structural enzyme proteins.

claims.claim_text: Beyond serving as a building block for protein biosynthesis, tryptophan is a biochemical precursor of serotonin (a neurotransmitter), which it forms via the enzyme tryptophan hydroxylase. Serotonin can in turn be converted to melatonin (a neurohormone). Tryptophan is also the raw material from which niacin is synthesized, by way of kynurenine and quinolinic acid intermediates. In plants it is even converted into the phytohormone auxin.
claims.verbatim:
Tryptophan is employed as a building block of protein
biosynthesis and is a biochemical precursor of serotonin (a neurotransmitter),
synthesized via tryptophan hydroxylase. Serotonin can be converted to melatonin
(a neurohormone); niacin is synthesized from tryptophan via kynurenine and
quinolinic acids as essential biosynthetic intermediates; auxin (a phytohormone)
is produced when sieve tube elements undergo apoptosis (programed cell-death),
tryptophan is converted to auxins.

claims.claim_text: The body can make niacin (vitamin B3) from tryptophan, and researchers measured how much is needed. When niacin status was gauged by urinary metabolite levels, the amount of supplementary tryptophan required to give the same response as one milligram of niacin ranged from 39 to 86 mg. By convention, 60 mg of tryptophan is treated as equivalent to one mg of niacin.
claims.verbatim:
When niacin status was gauged by urinary metablyte levels,
the quantities of supplementary tryptophan required to give the same response
as one mg of niacin ranged from 39 to 86 mg. Convention allows that 60 mg of
tryptophan is equivalent to one mg of niacin,

claims.claim_text: Phenylalanine and tryptophan compete for entry into the brain: phenylalanine employs the same active transport channel as tryptophan to cross the blood-brain barrier. As a result, large doses of phenylalanine will interfere with the production of serotonin, the neurotransmitter the brain makes from tryptophan.
claims.verbatim:
Phenylalanine employs the same active transport channel as tryptophan to cross
the blood-brain barrier, in large doses it will interfere with the production of
serotonin.

claims.claim_text: A metabolite of tryptophan called 5-HTP (5-hydroxytryptophan) has been suggested as a treatment for seizure disorders and depression. It acts quickly because it rapidly crosses the blood-brain barrier and is then rapidly decarboxylated into serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine, or 5-HT).
claims.verbatim:
A metabolite of tryptophan, S-hydroxytryptophan (S-HTP), has been
suggested as a treatment for seizure disorders and depression. It rapidly
crosses the blood brain barrier and is rapidly decarboxylated to serotonin (5-
hydroxytryptamine or 5-HT).

claims.claim_text: In 1989 there was a large tryptophan-associated outbreak of eosinophilia-myalgia syndrome (EMS) that caused at least 1,500 cases of permanent disability and at least 37 deaths. The problem was traced to a batch of L-tryptophan produced and exported to the United States by the Japanese manufacturer Showa Denko KK. The final explanation offered was that large doses of tryptophan gave rise to metabolites that inhibit the normal degradation of histamine, and that the resulting excess histamine caused EMS.
claims.verbatim:
In 1989 there was a large tryptophan-associated outbreak of eosinophilia-
myalgia syndrome (EMS) which caused at least 1,500 cases of permanent
disability and at least 37 deaths.

claims.claim_text: Tryptophan was first isolated in 1901 by Frederick Hopkins, who obtained it through the hydrolysis (chemical breakdown) of casein, the main protein found in milk.
claims.verbatim:
Tryptophan was isolated in 1901 by Frederick Hopkins via hydrolysis of
casein (milk protein).

claims.claim_text: Methionine is encoded by a single codon, AUG — and AUG is also the most common 'Start' signal in eukaryotic cells. When it sits within a Kozak consensus sequence, AUG tells a ribosome to begin translating a protein from messenger RNA (mRNA). Because that start signal is methionine's own codon, protein synthesis characteristically begins with a methionine residue, giving this amino acid a foundational role in assembling the body's proteins.
claims.verbatim:
The AUG codon is the most common eukaryote “Start”
message for a ribosome that signals the initiation of protein translation from
mRNA when the AUG codon is in a Kozak consensus sequence.

claims.claim_text: Wallach points to studies in which restricting dietary methionine increased the lifespan of laboratory animals. He highlights a study published in Nature showing that when fruit flies were kept on lifespan-extending calorie restriction, adding methionine back into their diet restored their fecundity (fertility) — yet did so without shortening the longer lifespans that calorie restriction normally produces. In effect, methionine governed fertility independently of the lifespan benefit.
claims.verbatim:
Some studies have shown that restriction of methionine can increase lifespans
of laboratory animals. A study, published in Nature, demonstrated that adding
methionine to the diets of fruit flies under dietary calorie restriction restored
fecundity without reducing the longer lifespans that are typical of dietary
restriction.

claims.claim_text: Wallach notes that methionine's role isn't limited to animals: plants use it as the starting material to synthesize ethylene — a plant hormone — through a pathway known as the Yang Cycle, or methionine cycle.
claims.verbatim:
Methionine is employed by plants for the synthesis of ethylene, the process is
known as the Yang Cycle or the methionine cycle.

claims.claim_text: Phenylalanine (abbreviated Phe) is one of the nine amino acids classically considered essential, meaning the human body cannot manufacture it and has to take it in from the diet. Chemically it is an alpha amino acid classified as nonpolar because of the water-repelling (hydrophobic) benzyl group on its side chain. It is one of the twenty amino acids the body uses to build the proteins encoded by DNA, and in the genetic code it is specified by the codons UUU and UUC. Beyond protein-building, phenylalanine is the raw material the body converts into tyrosine and, through it, several key signaling chemicals and pigments.
claims.verbatim:
Phenylalanine (Phe) is an alpha amino acid that is classified as nonpolar because
of the hydrophobic nature of its benzyl side chain. Phenylalanine is one of twenty
amino acids employed biochemically to synthesize proteins coded for by DNA.
The codons for phenylalanine are UUU and UUC.

claims.claim_text: Yes. Phenylalanine is one of the nine amino acids Wallach lists as classically 'essential': histidine, isoleucine, leucine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan, and valine. 'Essential' means the human body cannot synthesize these amino acids on its own, so they have to be consumed every day; without them, Wallach warns, deficiencies and their disease consequences follow. He also argues that three more amino acids—arginine, taurine, and tyrosine—should be treated as essential, because their long-term deficiency causes specific diseases too.
claims.verbatim:
There are nine amino acids that are classically considered to be “essential”
amino acids: Histidine, Isoleucine, leucine, Lysine, Methionine, Phenylalanine,
Threonine, Tryptophan and Valine. These amino acids can’t be synthesized
by humans and must be consumed on a daily basis to prevent deficiencies
and disease consequences.

claims.claim_text: Phenylalanine was first reported isolated in 1879 by the scientists Schulze and Barbieri, who obtained it from the yellow lupine plant (Lupinus luteus). A few years later, in 1882, Erlenmeyer and Lipp became the first to synthesize phenylalanine artificially, building it from phenylacetaldehyde, hydrogen cyanide, and ammonia.
claims.verbatim:
The first reports of the isolation of phenylalanine were made in 1879 by
Schulze and Barbieri, who isolated the amino acid from the yellow Lupine (Lupinus
luteus). In 1882, Erlenmeyer and Lipp first synthesized phenylalanine from
phenylacetaldehyde, hydrogen cyanide and ammonia.

claims.claim_text: Phenylketonuria (PKU) is an inborn error of metabolism in which the body cannot properly break down phenylalanine. Wallach takes the pointed position that PKU is 'falsely believed to be a genetically-transmitted disease.' Whatever its cause, he notes the practical management is the same: avoiding phenylalanine in the diet prevents the symptoms of PKU. This is why phenylalanine-containing products such as the sweetener aspartame carry warnings for people with the condition.
claims.verbatim:
The inborn error of metabolism known as phenylketonuria (PKU), falsely
believed to be a genetically-transmitted disease, is the inability to metabolize
phenylalanine. Avoidance of phenylalanine prevents the symptoms of PKU.

claims.claim_text: Yes. A major non-food source of phenylalanine is the artificial sweetener aspartame, sold under the brand names Equal and NutraSweet. When aspartame is metabolized it breaks down into several chemical byproducts, and one of them is phenylalanine. Because of this, aspartame-containing products in the United States, Canada, and Australia must be labeled 'Phenylketonurics: Contains phenylalanine'—a warning aimed at people with PKU who must avoid the amino acid.
claims.verbatim:
A non-food source of phenylalanine is the non-sugar sweetener aspartame
marketed as Equal and NutraSweet, both of which are metabolized into several
chemical byproducts including phenylalanine. Thus, all products in Australia, the
United States, and Canada that contain aspartame are labeled “Phenylketonurics:
Contains phenylalanine.”

claims.claim_text: DL-phenylalanine—a supplement form that combines the two mirror-image versions (D and L) of the amino acid—is marketed as a nutritional supplement for three main uses: as a sleep aid, as an anti-depressant, and as an analgesic, meaning a pain reliever. These uses line up with how phenylalanine shows up throughout Wallach's own protocols, where DL-phenylalanine is dosed for conditions ranging from depression and insomnia to nerve and movement disorders.
claims.verbatim:
DL-Phenylalanine is marketed as a nutritional supplement as a sleep aid, an
anti-depressant and as an analgesic (pain reliever).

claims.claim_text: Phenylalanine uses the same active transport channel as tryptophan to cross the blood-brain barrier—the protective filter that controls what enters the brain. Because the two amino acids compete for that same doorway, Wallach notes that phenylalanine in large doses will interfere with the production of serotonin, the mood- and sleep-related brain chemical the body makes from tryptophan. In effect, loading up on phenylalanine can push tryptophan out of the brain and blunt serotonin synthesis.
claims.verbatim:
Phenylalanine employs the same active transport channel as tryptophan to cross
the blood-brain barrier, in large doses it will interfere with the production of
serotonin.

claims.claim_text: Tyrosine (abbreviated Tyr) is one of the 22 amino acids that cells use to build proteins. Although mainstream science treats it as non-essential, Wallach adds tyrosine to the classic list of essential amino acids because a long-term deficiency drives a specific disease -- goiter. Beyond its role as a protein building block, tyrosine has a special chemistry thanks to its phenol group: it takes part in cellular signaling and, combined with the mineral iodine, is manufactured into the thyroid hormone thyroxin. It is also the precursor the body uses to make the neurotransmitters dopamine and norepinephrine, and the starting material for the pigment melanin.
claims.verbatim:
Tyrosine (Tyr ) is one of 22 amino acids that are employed by cells to synthesize
proteins; its codons are UAC and UAU.

claims.claim_text: The word 'tyrosine' comes from the Greek word for cheese. Wallach explains this is because the amino acid was first isolated from cheese, in 1846, by the German chemist Justus von Liebig. The name reflects where scientists first found the molecule rather than any special property of it -- a small piece of history that ties this thyroid- and brain-supporting amino acid back to a wheel of aged cheese.
claims.verbatim:
The origin of the word “tyrosine” is the
Greek word for cheese, as it was first isolated in 1846 from cheese by the German
chemist Justus von Liebig.

claims.claim_text: Beyond building proteins, tyrosine has a special job thanks to its phenol chemistry: it is a key player in signal transduction, the system cells use to relay messages internally. Tyrosine sits within signaling proteins where it acts as a receiver for phosphate groups, which enzymes called protein kinases transfer onto it. This phosphorylation of tyrosine's hydroxyl group changes the activity of the target protein, turning cellular processes up or down. Wallach notes that tyrosine phosphorylation is believed to be one of the key steps in signal transduction and in regulating enzyme activity.
claims.verbatim:
In addition to being a proteinogenic amino acid, tyrosine has a special function
because of its phenol functionality. Tyrosine is found in proteins that are part of
a signal transduction function. It acts as a receiver of phosphate groups that are
transferred by means of protein kinases. Phosphorylation of the hydroxyl group
alters the activity of the target protein.

claims.claim_text: Tyrosine matters in plants as well as animals. In plants it plays an essential role in photosynthesis: inside the chloroplasts, tyrosine acts as an electron donor that helps reduce, or re-charge, oxidized chlorophyll. In doing so it gives up a proton from its phenolic OH group, and the resulting radical is ultimately reduced back in photosystem II by the four core manganese clusters. It is a striking example of how the same amino acid serves completely different jobs across the living world.
claims.verbatim:
In plants, tyrosine residues play an essential role in photosynthesis. In
chloroplasts, tyrosine acts as an electron donor in the reduction of oxidized
chlorophyll. In this process tyrosine undergoes deprotonation of its phenolic OH-
group. This radical is ultimately reduced in the photosystem II by the four core
manganese clusters.

claims.claim_text: Lysine (abbreviated Lys) is one of the amino acids Wallach counts among the classic essentials: nutrients the human body cannot make on its own and must take in every day to prevent deficiency and disease. Chemically it is a base, like arginine and histidine, it takes part in hydrogen bonding, and it acts as a general base in catalysis; it is also a common site of methylation, producing methyl-, dimethyl-, and trimethyllysine. Its core job is protein production, and through its derivative allysine it is essential for building the collagen and elastin that hold connective tissue and blood vessels together. Lysine is encoded by the DNA codons AAA and AAG.
claims.verbatim:
Lysine (Lys) is an essential amino acid with the codons AAA and AAG. Lysine is
a base, as are arginine and histidine. Lysine participates in hydrogen bonding
and a general base in catalysis. Common post-translational modifications of lysine
include methylation producing methyl-, dimethyl-, and trimethyllysine.

claims.claim_text: In mammals, lysine is broken down to produce acetyl-CoA, a key molecule that feeds the body's central energy-generating pathways. Wallach notes that this breakdown begins with an initial transamination, a reaction in which lysine hands off its nitrogen-containing amino group to alpha-ketoglutarate.
claims.verbatim:
Lysine in mammals is metabolized to produce acetyl-CoA through an initial
transamination with alpha ketogluterate.

claims.claim_text: To illustrate how vital an essential amino acid is, Wallach points to the 1993 film Jurassic Park (from Michael Crichton's 1990 novel), in which dinosaurs are recreated by DNA engineering. In the story the dinosaurs are deliberately altered so they cannot produce their own lysine, the so-called 'lysine contingency', which would keep them from surviving outside the park and force them to depend on lysine supplements provided by the park's supplement program. The plot device works precisely because lysine is essential: an animal that cannot make it and is not fed it will not survive.
claims.verbatim:
the dinosaurs were altered so that they could not produce lysine (the “lysine
contingency”) that would prevent the dinosaurs survival outside of the park

claims.claim_text: Lysine is one of the nine amino acids that Wallach, following the classic classification, calls 'essential': histidine, isoleucine, leucine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan, and valine. What makes them essential is that the human body cannot synthesize them on its own, so they must be consumed on a daily basis to prevent deficiencies and their disease consequences. Wallach further argues that three more amino acids, arginine, taurine, and tyrosine, should be treated as essential too, because long-term shortages of them drive cancer, macular degeneration, and goiter respectively.
claims.verbatim:
There are nine amino acids that are classically considered to be “essential”
amino acids: Histidine, Isoleucine, leucine, Lysine, Methionine, Phenylalanine,
Threonine, Tryptophan and Valine. These amino acids can’t be synthesized
by humans and must be consumed on a daily basis to prevent deficiencies
and disease consequences.

claims.claim_text: Leucine (abbreviated Leu) is a branched-chain alpha amino acid that Wallach classifies as hydrophobic, meaning it avoids water and tends to tuck into the interior of proteins. It is unusual in being specified by six different genetic codons (UUA, UUG, CUU, CUC, CUA, and CUG), more than most amino acids, and it makes up a significant part of the subunits of ferritin and astacin, as well as a class of so-called 'buffer' proteins. That structural profile is part of why leucine is woven throughout the body's core protein machinery rather than serving one narrow role.
claims.verbatim:
Leucine (Leu) is a branched chain alpha amino acid that is classified as a
hydrophobic amino acid. It has six codons (UUA, UUG, CUU, CUC, CUA, and CUG)
and is a significant part of the subunits of ferritin, astacin, and a class of “buffer”
proteins.

claims.claim_text: Leucine is the amino acid Wallach ties most directly to muscle. He describes it as a catalyst for muscle growth and muscle 'insurance,' and says it activates the mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) kinase, the cellular switch that regulates cell growth. Read alongside his point that leucine is solely responsible for the synthesis of muscle proteins, this is why leucine is the branched-chain amino acid most associated with building and protecting muscle tissue.
claims.verbatim:
Leucine is important as a catalysts for muscle growth and muscle “insurance.”
Additionally, leucine activates the mammalian target of rapamycin kinase that
regulates cell growth.

claims.claim_text: Wallach places leucine's major functions in three tissues: the liver, the adipose (fat) tissue, and muscle. In both muscle and adipose tissue leucine is used to synthesize sterols—the fat-like building blocks that include cholesterol and steroid compounds—and he notes that leucine's combined use across muscle and fat is actually larger than the amount used by the liver. So while the liver is the usual hub of amino-acid metabolism, for leucine the muscle and fat tissues do the heavier work.
claims.verbatim:
Leucine has major functions in the liver, adipose tissue, and muscle. In muscle
and adipose tissue, leucine is employed to synthesize sterols and its combined use
in these tissues is larger than that used by the liver.

claims.claim_text: Leucine is not harmless in excess. Wallach warns that leucine toxicity—seen when Maple Syrup Urine Disease (MSUD) becomes decompensated, meaning the body can no longer keep the amino acid in check—produces delirium and neurologic compromise and can be life-threatening. MSUD is the classic picture of what happens when branched-chain amino acids like leucine build up unchecked, and it is why leucine, for all its muscle benefits, carries a genuine upper limit.
claims.verbatim:
Leucine toxicity, manifested as in decompensated Maple Syrup Urine Disease
(MSUD), produces delirium, neurologic compromise and can be life threatening.

claims.claim_text: According to Wallach, too much leucine can produce a clinical pellagra, identified by the classic 'four D's': diarrhea, dermatitis, dementia, and death. Pellagra is normally associated with a shortage of niacin, so it is striking that Wallach flags an excess of leucine—not a shortage of anything—as a cause. It is a pointed caution that with leucine, more is not automatically better and that intake has a real ceiling.
claims.verbatim:
Excessive leucine intake can produce clinical pellagra ("the four D's"), ie.,
diarrhea, dermatitis, dementia, and death.

claims.claim_text: Leucine is one of the nine amino acids Wallach counts as classically 'essential': histidine, isoleucine, leucine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan, and valine. 'Essential' here has a precise meaning—the human body cannot synthesize these amino acids on its own, so they must be consumed on a daily basis to prevent deficiencies and the disease consequences that follow. (Wallach separately argues that arginine, taurine, and tyrosine should be added to this classic list, but leucine sits squarely inside the traditional nine.)
claims.verbatim:
There are nine amino acids that are classically considered to be “essential”
amino acids: Histidine, Isoleucine, leucine, Lysine, Methionine, Phenylalanine,
Threonine, Tryptophan and Valine. These amino acids can’t be synthesized
by humans and must be consumed on a daily basis to prevent deficiencies
and disease consequences.

claims.claim_text: Valine is one of the nine amino acids Wallach classifies as classically 'essential': histidine, isoleucine, leucine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan, and valine. Calling it essential means the human body cannot synthesize (make) valine on its own, so it must be consumed from the diet on a daily basis. Without that steady daily intake, Wallach warns, deficiencies and their disease consequences follow.
claims.verbatim:
There are nine amino acids that are classically considered to be “essential”
amino acids: Histidine, Isoleucine, leucine, Lysine, Methionine, Phenylalanine,
Threonine, Tryptophan and Valine. These amino acids can’t be synthesized
by humans and must be consumed on a daily basis to prevent deficiencies
and disease consequences.

claims.claim_text: Valine is a branched-chain amino acid, and its name comes from valerian, the flowering plant. It was first isolated in 1901 by the German chemist Emil Fischer, who extracted it from casein — the principal protein in milk.
claims.verbatim:
Valine is a branched chain amino acid that was named for the plant valerian. In
1901 valine was isolated from casein by Emil Fischer.

claims.claim_text: At the chemical level, valine—abbreviated 'Val'—is an alpha amino acid, the standard structural form the body uses to build proteins. In the genetic code it is specified by four codons: GUU, GUC, GUA, and GUG, meaning any one of these three-letter genetic sequences directs a cell to add valine to a protein it is building.
claims.verbatim: Valine (Val) is an alpha amino acid with the codons GUU, GUC, GUA, and GUG.

claims.claim_text: Wallach points to valine's role in sickle-cell disease as an example of how a single amino-acid substitution changes a protein. In this condition, valine substitutes for glutamic acid within hemoglobin, the oxygen-carrying protein of red blood cells. Because glutamic acid is hydrophilic (water-loving) and valine is hydrophobic (water-repelling), swapping one for the other alters the protein's behavior in water and makes the hemoglobin more likely to aggregate—to clump together.
claims.verbatim:
In sickle-cell disease, valine can substitute for the hydrophilic amino acid
glutamic acid in hemoglobin. Valine is hydrophobic; therefore the hemoglobin is
more likely to aggregate.

claims.claim_text: Wallach counts histidine among the nine amino acids classically considered "essential" -- alongside isoleucine, leucine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan, and valine. "Essential" means the body cannot synthesize these on its own, so they must be consumed every day through the diet; without them, Wallach warns, deficiencies and specific disease consequences follow. (He separately argues that arginine, taurine, and tyrosine should be added to this classic list, because their long-term deficiency also produces specific diseases.)
claims.verbatim:
There are nine amino acids that are classically considered to be “essential”
amino acids: Histidine, Isoleucine, leucine, Lysine, Methionine, Phenylalanine,
Threonine, Tryptophan and Valine. These amino acids can’t be synthesized
by humans and must be consumed on a daily basis to prevent deficiencies
and disease consequences.

claims.claim_text: According to the Epigenetics account, histidine was first isolated in 1896 by the German physician Albrecht Kossel. It is one of the 22 proteinogenic amino acids -- the building blocks the body strings together to make its proteins.
claims.verbatim:
Histidine was first
isolated in 1896 by the German physician Albrecht Kossel.

claims.claim_text: Histidine's chemistry comes from its imidazole side chain. That ring makes histidine a coordinating ligand of metalloproteins -- it binds and holds metal atoms -- and places it at the catalytic sites of certain enzymes. In a catalytic triad, the basic nitrogen of histidine abstracts (pulls away) a proton from a nearby serine, threonine, or cysteine, activating that residue as a nucleophile so it can attack and break chemical bonds. The same imidazole also lets histidine act as a proton shuttle, moving hydrogen ions quickly where they are needed.
claims.verbatim:
The imidazole sidechain of histidine is a coordinating ligand of
metalloproteins and is a part of catalytic sites in certain enzymes. In catalytic
triads, the basic nitrogen of histidine is used to abstract a proton from serine,
threonine, or cysteine to activate it as a nucleophile.

claims.claim_text: Isoleucine (abbreviated Ile) is an alpha amino acid and one of the nine amino acids classically considered essential, meaning the human body cannot make it and it must come from the diet every day. Its hydrocarbon side chain makes it a hydrophobic amino acid, and it is carried on the genetic codons AUU, AUC, and AUA. In Wallach's table of essential amino-acid functions, isoleucine's role is protein production.
claims.verbatim:
Isoleucine (Ile) is an alpha amino acid with the codons AUU, AUC, and AUA. As
a result of its hydrocarbon side chain, isoleucine is classed as a hydrophobic
amino acid.

claims.claim_text: Isoleucine is one of the nine amino acids classically considered essential, alongside histidine, leucine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan, and valine. Wallach explains that because the human body cannot synthesize these amino acids on its own, they must be consumed on a daily basis to prevent deficiencies and their disease consequences.
claims.verbatim:
There are nine amino acids that are classically considered to be “essential”
amino acids: Histidine, Isoleucine, leucine, Lysine, Methionine, Phenylalanine,
Threonine, Tryptophan and Valine. These amino acids can’t be synthesized
by humans and must be consumed on a daily basis to prevent deficiencies
and disease consequences.

claims.claim_text: Isoleucine was first isolated in 1903 by Felix Ehrlich, a German chemist, who obtained it from hemoglobin—the oxygen-carrying protein of red blood cells.
claims.verbatim:
In 1903 Felix Ehrlich, a German chemist, isolated isoleucine from
hemoglobin.

claims.claim_text: Wallach places threonine on the classic list of nine "essential" amino acids—alongside histidine, isoleucine, leucine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, tryptophan, and valine. "Essential" carries a precise meaning here: the human body cannot synthesize these amino acids on its own, so they have to be supplied through the diet every single day. Wallach's point is that falling short of them does not just cause a shortage on paper—it leads to real deficiencies and their disease consequences, which is why he treats the daily intake of threonine and its fellow essentials as non-negotiable.
claims.verbatim:
There are nine amino acids that are classically considered to be “essential”
amino acids: Histidine, Isoleucine, leucine, Lysine, Methionine, Phenylalanine,
Threonine, Tryptophan and Valine. These amino acids can’t be synthesized
by humans and must be consumed on a daily basis to prevent deficiencies
and disease consequences.

claims.claim_text: Wallach describes threonine as biochemically busy in two ways. First, once it is part of a protein, the threonine residue is a target for numerous post-translational modifications—chemical tags added by glycosylation and by phosphorylation through the enzyme threonine kinase. Second, threonine is actively broken down for energy: threonine dehydrogenase converts it to pyruvate, and an intermediate in that pathway can react with coenzyme A (thiolysis) to yield acetyl-CoA and glycine. Alternatively, threonine can be converted to alpha-ketobutyrate by serine dehydrogenase, feeding into the succinyl-CoA pathway.
claims.verbatim:
The threonine
residue is susceptible to numerous post-translational modifications; it can undergo
glycosylation and phosphorylation through the action of threonine kinase.
Threonine is converted to pyruvate via threonine dehydrogenase, an

intermediate in this pathway can undergo thiolysis with CoA to produce acetyl-
CoA and glycine; it can also be converted to alpha ketobutyrate via the enzyme
serine dehydrogenase entering the pathway leading to succinyl-CoA.

claims.claim_text: In one fatty-acid overview Wallach names the essential fatty acids as linoleic, linolenic, and arachidonic, and says these are further divided into omega-3 (which he lists as DHA and EPA), omega-6, omega-9, and cholesterol. This is the single place he slots omega-9 into the omega grouping alongside the others. It is worth reading against his dominant stance in the same book and elsewhere, where he states that only two fatty acids are classically regarded as essential -- alpha-linolenic acid (an omega-3) and linoleic acid (an omega-6) -- so he does not label omega-9 itself essential.
claims.verbatim:
Essential fatty acids include the linoleic, linolenic and arachadonic fatty acids,
which are further divided into the Omega-3 (DHA and EPA), Omega-6, Omega-9,
and cholesterol.

claims.claim_text: Wallach lays out four types of mineral colloid, and the third is the one he describes as the most stable form found in nature. In it, carbon itself forms the protective coating around the mineral, a molecular chain roughly 10 to 12 carbon atoms long. He notes this carbon-coated colloid also occurs in bacteria, fungi, plants (including some forms of petrified wood), animals and humans. It is this carbon-coated type that he calls the most stable of the naturally occurring organic mineral colloids.
claims.verbatim:
The third type of organic mineral colloid has a protective coating of
carbon with a molecular chain length of 10 to 12 carbon atoms. This
type of colloid is also found in bacteria, fungi, plants (including some
forms of petrified wood), animals and humans and is thought to be the
most stable form of naturally occurring organic mineral colloids.

claims.claim_text: Beyond the two classically essential fatty acids, Wallach identifies a 'conditionally essential' group of fats. He places three fatty acids in it: arachidonic acid and gamma-linolenic acid, which are both omega-6 fatty acids, and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA), which is an omega-3. So two of the three fatty acids Wallach calls conditionally essential are omega-6 forms.
claims.verbatim:
Some fatty acids are classified as “conditionally essential.” This group includes:
arachidonic acid (an omega-6 fatty acid), docosahexaenoic acid (an omega-3 fatty
acid) and gamma-linolenic acid (an omega-6 fatty acid).

claims.claim_text: Wallach recounts that the two essential fatty acids -- omega-3 (linolenic) and omega-6 (linoleic) -- were identified in 1923 and were originally listed as 'vitamin F.' In 1929, laboratory rat studies showed the two fatty acids were more properly classed as fats rather than vitamins, so the vitamin label was dropped. It is a piece of nutritional history explaining why these fats were once grouped with the vitamins.
claims.verbatim:
In 1923 the two essential fatty acids were identified, but they were originally
listed as “vitamin F." In 1929 laboratory rat studies indicated that these two fatty
acids were more properly classed as fats rather than being listed as vitamins.

claims.claim_text: Wallach teaches that in the human body the essential fatty acids serve many functions, and all of them require a proper ratio between the omega-3 and omega-6 forms. So getting enough omega-6 is not the whole story -- it has to be in the right balance with omega-3 for those functions to work correctly. He points to traditional diets, which contained nearly equal amounts of omega-3 and omega-6, as the model of that balance.
claims.verbatim:
In the human body the essential fatty acids serve multiple functions, all of
which require proper ratios between omega-3 and omega-6 forms.

claims.claim_text: Wallach explains that the essential fatty acids are required to produce and maintain a whole family of signaling compounds: eicosanoids, endocannabinoids (which affect mood, behavior and inflammation), lipoxins and resolvins. He specifies that lipoxins -- a class of eicosanoid derivatives made through the lipoxygenase pathway -- come from omega-6 EFAs, while resolvins come from omega-3. So omega-6 is not just a structural fat; it is a starting material the body converts into inflammation- and signaling-regulating molecules.
claims.verbatim:
The fatty acids are required for the production and maintenance of
eicosanoids, endocannabinoids (affecting mood, behavior, and inflammation),
lipoxins (a class of eicosanoid derivatives through the lipoxygenase pathway
from omega-6 EFAs), and resolvins from omega-3 (in the presence of
aspirin, downregulating inflammation)

claims.claim_text: Wallach explains that gallium and ferric (iron) salts behave similarly in biological systems, so gallium ions frequently mimic iron ions in medical applications. Because of that chemical resemblance, gallium can slip into the same biological pathways the body normally uses for iron. He places gallium in the same chemical family as aluminum, but it is this iron-like behavior that gives the metal a role in medicine.
claims.verbatim:
Because gallium and ferric salts behave similarly
in biological systems, gallium ions often mimic iron ions in medical applications.

claims.claim_text: Wallach points to gallium maltolate -- an orally absorbable form of the gallium(III) ion -- as a form of the mineral used in real medical treatments. He says it is applied against brain cancer, inflammation, and certain infectious diseases. That therapeutic use backs his broader argument that gallium has a genuine biological role, not merely a place on the periodic table.
claims.verbatim:
Gallium maltolate, an orally
absorbable form of gallium (Ill) ion, is used in medical treatments for brain cancer,
inflammation, and certain infectious diseases.

claims.claim_text: Wallach catalogs where gallium turns up in nature: about 15 ppm in igneous rocks, 19 ppm in shale, 12 ppm in sandstone, and just 4 ppm in limestone, thinning to tiny fractions of a part per million in fresh and sea water. In living things the levels fall further -- roughly 0.5 ppm in marine plants and animals but only 0.06 ppm in land plants and 0.006 ppm in land animals. He adds that gallium occurs in nature only as trace amounts in bauxite and zinc ores.
claims.verbatim:
Ga - Gallium is found in igneous rocks at 15 ppm; shale at 19 ppm; sandstone
at 12 ppm; limestone at 4 ppm; fresh water at 0.001 ppm; sea water at 0.00003
ppm; soils at 0.4 to 6.0 ppm to 30.0 ppm; marine plants at 0.5 ppm; land plants
at 0.06 ppm; marine animals at 0.5 ppm; and land animals at 0.006 ppm.
Gallium (Ill) is found in nature as trace amounts in bauxite and zinc ores.

claims.claim_text: Wallach holds that aluminum is remarkably nontoxic, and backs it with hard toxicology: aluminum sulfate has an oral LD50 (the dose that kills half of test animals) of 6207 mg/kg in mice, which for an 80 kg person works out to about 500 grams - more than a pound of it - in a single day. He stresses that aluminum is not nearly as toxic as the true heavy metals, so the trace amounts in ordinary food and water are nowhere near a harmful level.
claims.verbatim:
Aluminum is remarkably nontoxic, aluminum sulfate having an LDSO of 6207
mg/kg (oral/mouse), which would be the equivalent of 500 grams (more than a
pound) for an 80 kg human per day.

claims.claim_text: According to Wallach, studies show that everyday aluminum products - cookware, deodorants, and antiperspirants - are generally safe when used at directed levels, and there is no evidence that aluminum in food or liquid causes any disease, including Alzheimer's. He notes one caveat: a small percentage of people are sensitive to aluminum and have reported contact dermatitis and digestive disorders after ingesting aluminum-containing products. For everyone else, he says the toxicity studies show it simply isn't harmful.
claims.verbatim:
Studies have shown
that aluminum cookware, deodorants, and antiperspirants are generally safe at
directed levels. There is no evidence that exposure to aluminum in food or liquid
causes any diseases, including Alzheimer's disease.

claims.claim_text: Wallach flags one genuine trade-off with aluminum: it can compete with calcium for absorption. When the amount of dietary aluminum climbs, that competition can reduce skeletal mineralization - a thinning or under-mineralization of bone he calls osteopenia. So while he considers aluminum broadly nontoxic, he notes that an elevated dietary aluminum load can still come at the expense of bone.
claims.verbatim:
Aluminum can compete with calcium absorption, and increased amounts of
dietary aluminum can result in reduced skeletal mineralization (osteopenia).

claims.claim_text: Wallach traces the metal's name to Sir Humphrey Davy, the English chemist who dubbed it 'the metal of clay' - aluminum. The clay connection runs through its whole story: European chemists in the early 1700s realized a light-weight metal was locked inside clay, and a particularly rich aluminum-bearing clay found at Las Baux in France gave its ore, 'Bauxite,' its name.
claims.verbatim:
Sir Humphrey Davy, a distinguished English chemist of the 16th century gave
the name “aluminum’ to the metal of clay.

claims.claim_text: Wallach explains that aluminum never shows up as a free metal in nature - it is always bound tightly to oxygen as a hard oxide called alumina. When that alumina picks up traces of other elements it turns into gemstones: rubies and sapphires are essentially colored aluminum oxide. Those same gems, he notes, have been used as medicine for thousands of years in Ayurvedic practice.
claims.verbatim:
Aluminum does not occur as a free metal in nature, but is found only in
tight combination with oxygen forming a hard oxide known as alumina, When
contaminated with traces of other elements, alumina becomes a gem, such as
rubies or sapphires, which in addition to being used as jewelry, these gems have
also been used as medicine for thousands of years in the practice of Ayruvedic
medicine.

claims.claim_text: Wallach documents that gold is spread only in tiny traces through the natural world -- roughly 0.004 ppm in igneous and sedimentary rocks, 0.00006 ppm in fresh water, and just 0.000011 ppm in sea water, with even smaller amounts in marine and land plants and animals. Among plants, gold specifically concentrates in the horsetail plant, and in mammalian livers it forms a colloid. The vanishingly small figures show how rare and dilute gold is in living tissue.
claims.verbatim:
Au - Gold is found in igneous and sedimentary rocks at 0.004 ppm; fresh water
at 0.00006 ppm; sea water at 0.000011 ppm; marine plants at 0.012 ppm; land
plants at 0.0005 to 0.002 ppm (gold concentrates in the horse tail plant); marine
animals at 0.0003 to 0.008 ppm; land animals 0.00023 and in mammalian livers
it will form a colloid.

claims.claim_text: Wallach recounts that in medieval times gold was widely seen as beneficial to human health -- believed to be the most noble of substances and the 'panacea,' a medicine thought to treat all disease. He notes the 'alchemists,' whom he calls the earliest of chemists, spent most of their efforts trying to transmute lead and other base metals into gold. That drive to turn cheap metals into gold shaped much of early chemistry.
claims.verbatim:
In medieval times, gold was often seen as beneficial for human health, with
the belief that it was the most noble of substances and would be the “panacea” or
medicine that would treat all disease. The “alchemists,” the earliest of chemists,
spent most of their efforts in trying to transmute lead and other base metals into
gold.

claims.claim_text: Wallach describes an ancient Chinese belief that gold itself was immortal and that consuming it could make a person immortal as well. A practical obstacle, he explains, was that gold powder could not be absorbed and passed through the intestinal tract unchanged, so alchemists searched for ways to make it usable. The conviction ran so deep that the Chinese held it was enough simply to eat meals each day from plates made of alloys that merely looked like gold in order to gain immortality.
claims.verbatim:
The Chinese believed it was sufficient to eat meals each day from plates made
of alloys that looked like gold to gain immortality.

claims.claim_text: Wallach warns that gold therapies carry a wide range of toxic reactions. Milder ones include pruritus (itching), dermatitis, stomatitis (inflammation of the mouth), and gastrointestinal (GI) discomfort, along with increased albumin or blood in the urine. More serious reactions can involve aplastic anemia, a drop in white blood cell count, hepatitis, and pneumonitis (lung inflammation).
claims.verbatim:
Toxic reactions to gold therapies include pruritus (itching), dermatitis,
stomatitis, Gl discomfort, increase in urine albumin, blood in the urine, aplastic
anemia, reduced WBC, hepatitis, and pneumonitis.

claims.claim_text: Wallach recounts that bromine was discovered independently by two chemists: Carl Jacob Lowig in 1825 and Antoine Balard in 1826. Balard isolated it from the ash of seaweed gathered in the salt marshes of Montpellier — seaweed that was being processed to obtain iodine but which also happened to contain bromine. Lowig, working separately, isolated it from a mineral-water spring in his hometown of Bad Kreuznach.
claims.verbatim:
Bromine was discovered independently by two chemists, Carl Jacob Lowig
(1825) and Antoine Balard (1826). Balard isolated bromine from the ash of
seaweed collected from the salt marshes of Montpellier. The seaweed was used
to obtain iodine but it also contained bromine. Lowig isolated bromine from a
mineral water spring from his hometown of Bad Kreuznach.

claims.claim_text: Wallach notes that toxic reactions from a bromine overdose can resemble acne-like skin eruptions. He places this alongside bromine's long history as a sedative: compounds such as potassium bromide were used as sedatives through the 19th and 20th centuries, and the FDA later removed over-the-counter sedatives such as Bromo-Seltzer from public sale in 1975.
claims.verbatim: Toxic reactions from an overdose can resemble acne-like skin eruptions.

claims.claim_text: Lanthanum, chemical symbol La, is what Dr. Wallach calls a 'light' rare earth metal, one of the rare earths he groups with the 'cerium metals' (lanthanum, cerium, praseodymium, neodymium, illinium, samarium). He describes it as widely but extremely thinly spread through nature: roughly 30 ppm in igneous rocks and soil, about 20 ppm in shale, only a trace (0.000012 ppm) in seawater, and around 0.085 ppm in land plants. Despite being classed with the exotic 'rare earths,' Wallach lists it among the essential elements the human body should be getting.
claims.verbatim:
La - Lanthanum is a “light” rare earth metal and is found in igneous rocks at
30 ppm; shale at 20 ppm; sandstone at 7.5 ppm; limestone at 6.2 ppm; sea
water at 0.000012 ppm; soil at 30 ppm; marine plants at 10 ppm; land plants at
0.085 ppm

claims.claim_text: According to Wallach, lanthanum does turn up in living tissue, but only in tiny amounts and unevenly. In land animals he reports just 0.0001 ppm in soft tissue against 0.27 ppm in bone, meaning it concentrates in the skeleton far more than in the rest of the body. He also finds it in marine mammals (about 0.1 ppm), so in his data lanthanum appears across animal life at trace levels and preferentially in bone.
claims.verbatim:
mammals at 0.1 ppm; land animals at 0.0001 ppm in soft tissue and 0.27 ppm in
bone.

claims.claim_text: In Wallach's framework cerium is one of the Rare Earth elements, and he singles it out as the most abundant of all the rare earths. Its name comes from the dwarf planet Ceres, which was itself named after the Roman goddess of agriculture. Wallach lists cerium among the roughly 60 essential elements, metals and minerals he holds the body needs, treating it as a plant-derived trace mineral rather than a useless curiosity.
claims.verbatim:
Cerium was named for the dwarf planet Ceres (which was named after the
Roman goddess of agriculture). Cerium is the most abundant form of the rare
earth elements.

claims.claim_text: Cerium was first identified in 1803. Wallach records that it was discovered at Bastnas in Sweden by Jons Jakob Berzelius and Wilhelm Hisinger, and also in Germany by Martin Heinrich Klaproth the same year. He describes cerium as the most abundant of the rare-earth elements.
claims.verbatim:
Cerium was discovered in Bastnas in Sweden by Jons Jakob
Berzelius and Wihelm Hisinger and also in Germany by Martin Heinrich Klaproth
in 1803.

claims.claim_text: Cerium is a plant-derived trace mineral in Wallach's system. He notes it is commonly found in tobacco plants, in barley, and in the wood of beech trees. Land plants can concentrate it strongly — accumulating cerium up to 320 ppm — which is part of why he counts it among the plant-sourced minerals worth getting into the diet.
claims.verbatim:
Cerium can
be commonly found in tobacco plants, barley, and in the wood of beech trees.

claims.claim_text: In Wallach's framework beryllium is one of the essential minerals, and his books describe it as a relatively rare element in both the universe and the earth's crust. Chemically it is a divalent metal that never occurs free in nature, showing up only bound into alloys or minerals, and it heads the 'alkaline-earth' family alongside calcium and magnesium. In pure form it is a hard, gray-white metal - one of the lightest metals, yet hard enough to scratch glass - and so reactive that it readily combines with oxygen and other elements. You mostly encounter it inside gemstones such as beryl, emerald, aquamarine and chrysoberyl.
claims.verbatim:
Beryllium is a relatively rare element in the universe and the crust of the earth.
It is a divalent element that occurs naturally only in alloys with other elements
or minerals. Gemstones that contain beryllium include beryl (aquamarine and
emeralds) and chrysoberyl.

claims.claim_text: Beryllium was first isolated in 1798 by the French chemist Louis-Nicolas Vauquelin, who reported to the Institut de France that he had found a new 'rare earth' by dissolving aluminum hydroxide out of emerald and beryl with an added alkali. Because some of the new substance's compounds tasted sweet, the editors of the journal Annales de Chimie et de Physique named it 'glucine.' In Wallach's telling, beryllium entered chemistry already labeled a rare earth pulled straight out of gemstones.
claims.verbatim:
In a 1798 paper read before the Institut de France, Louis-Nicolas Vauquelin
reported that he had found a new “rare earth” by dissolving aluminum hydroxide
from emerald and beryl in an additional alkali. The editors of the journal Annales
de Chimie et de Physique named the new rare earth “glucine” for the sweet taste
of some of its compounds.

claims.claim_text: For most of its history the element was not called beryllium at all. Because beryllium and many of its compounds have a distinctly sweet taste, it was first named 'glucine,' and for about 160 years it was known as glucinum or glucinium - from the Greek word for sweet - carrying the chemical symbol Gl. Martin Heinrich Klaproth preferred the name 'beryllina' because the rare earth yttria also formed sweet salts, and the modern term 'beryllium' was first used by Wohler in 1828.
claims.verbatim:
Martin Heinrich Klaproth preferred the name “beryllina” due to the fact that
yttria also formed sweet salts. The term “beryllium” was first used by Wohler in
1828. For about 160 years, beryllium was also known as glucinum, or glucinium
with the chemical symbol of Gl, the naming derived from the Greek word sweet
for the sweet taste of the pure substance.

claims.claim_text: Rubidium (symbol Rb) is a trace mineral that Wallach places among 'The 60 Essential Elements, Metals, Minerals, Trace Minerals and Rare Earths' — the full roster of inorganic nutrients he holds the body requires. He groups it with the essential minerals found in high-quality humic shale, the plant-derived colloidal minerals he recommends to replace minerals stripped from modern food. Although rubidium is not 'classically' considered essential, Wallach argues it meets two or more of the criteria for an essential nutrient, so in his framework it belongs on the list of elements people need rather than being dismissed as a throwaway trace element.
claims.verbatim:
The 60 Essential Elements, Metals, Minerals, Trace Minerals and Rare Earths


Aluminum Gold Rhenium
Arsenic Hafnium Rubidium

claims.claim_text: Wallach documents rubidium throughout the natural world — in igneous rocks, shale, sandstone, soil, fresh and sea water, and in both marine and land plants and animals, with land plants at 20 ppm. In land animals it concentrates most heavily in the liver and muscle, and least of all in bone, a distribution he specifically calls out. That places rubidium in living tissue rather than only in geology, consistent with his view that it belongs among the plant-derived trace minerals the body requires.
claims.verbatim:
Rb - Rubidium is found in igneous rocks at 90 ppm; shale at 140 ppm; sandstone
at 60 ppm; limestone at 3 ppm; fresh water at 0.0015 ppm; sea water at 0.12
ppm; soil at 100 ppm (fixed by clay soils); marine plants at 7.4 ppm; land plants
at 20 ppm; marine animals at 20 ppm; land animals at 17 ppm (highest levels in
liver and muscle; lowest levels in bone).

claims.claim_text: In Wallach's survey of the rare earths, erbium is not confined to rock — it moves into living things. He reports that in land animals erbium is stored primarily in bone, while land plants take it up strongly, reaching as much as 46 parts per million in the hickory tree (Carya species). It also turns up in marine animals at 0.02 to 0.04 ppm, and in igneous rock, shale, sandstone and limestone at progressively lower levels. That plants concentrate erbium so heavily fits Wallach's larger view that trace and rare-earth minerals are meant to reach us through plant-derived sources.
claims.verbatim:
Er - Erbium, a rare earth metal, is found in igneous rock at 2.8 ppm; shale at
1.9 ppm; sandstone at 1 ppm; limestone at 0.36 ppm; land plants up to 46 ppm
in Carya spp.; marine animals at 0.02 to 0.04 ppm and land animals primarily in
bone.

claims.claim_text: Wallach describes europium as a 'light' rare-earth metal spread thinly through the environment -- roughly 1 to 2 ppm in igneous rock, about 1.1 ppm in shale, and even less in sandstone and limestone. Living things take it up: land plants hold around 0.021 ppm but can accumulate up to 16 ppm in the hickory tree (Carya spp.), and marine animals carry 0.01 to 0.06 ppm. In land animals europium barely registers in soft tissue (0.00012 ppm) yet concentrates in bone at 0.2 ppm -- the same skeletal pattern Wallach notes for its sister rare earths erbium and dysprosium, which also settle primarily in the bones.
claims.verbatim:
Eu - Europium is a “light” rare earth metal found in igneous rock at 1 to 2 ppm;
shale at 1.1 ppm; sandstone at 0.55 ppm; limestone at 0.2 ppm; land plants at
0.021 ppm (accumulates up to 16 ppm in Carya spp.); marine animals at 0.01 to
0.06 ppm; land animals at 0.00012 ppm in soft tissue and 0.2 ppm in bone.

claims.claim_text: The road to isolating europium ran through the study of how rare earths glow. In the late 1880s William Crookes observed the phosphorescent spectra of the rare-earth elements; even so, the discovery of europium is generally credited to the French chemist Eugene-Anatole Demarcay, who succeeded in isolating it in 1901. Wallach elsewhere notes that Demarcay named the new element for the continent of Europe.
claims.verbatim:
In the late 1880s William Crookes observed the phosphorescent spectra of the
rare earth elements; however, the discovery of europium is generally credited to
the French chemist Eugene-Anatole Demarcay, who isolated europium in 1901.

claims.claim_text: In Wallach's rundown of where cesium occurs, it is spread thinly across the whole natural world, from igneous rock, shale, sandstone and limestone to fresh and sea water, soils, plants and animals, always at very low trace levels. Marine plants carry about 0.07 ppm and land plants about 0.2 ppm, and it also turns up in living animals: land animals hold roughly 0.064 ppm, with the highest concentrations found in the muscle. The point is that cesium is not just a mineral locked in rock and soil; living plant and animal tissue actually take it up, however faintly.
claims.verbatim:
Cs - Cesium (caesium) is found in igneous rocks at 1 ppm; shale at 5 ppm;
sandstone and limestone at 0.5 ppm; fresh water at 0.0002 ppm; sea water at
0.00005 ppm; soils at 0.3 to 25 ppm; marine plants at 0.07 ppm. Land plants at

0.2 ppm; and land animals at 0.064 ppm (highest concentrations in the muscle).
tags: is cesium found in the body

claims.claim_text: Wallach traces barium's name to the old alchemy term 'baryta,' which itself comes from the Greek word 'barys,' meaning 'heavy.' It is a fitting name: barium's two most common naturally occurring minerals are barite (barium sulfate) and witherite (barium carbonate), both insoluble in water, and barium sulfate is such a dense salt that it blocks X-rays and is swallowed to outline the gut in medical imaging.
claims.verbatim:
Barium’s
name is derived from the alchemy “baryta” which comes from the Greek word
barys, which translates as “heavy.”

claims.claim_text: According to Wallach, barium was first isolated as an element in 1774, but it was not classed as a metal until 1808. In his other books he credits the English chemist Sir Humphry Davy with barium in 1808. Long before chemists isolated the element, barium was familiar through its ore minerals — barite, a barium sulfate, and witherite, a barium carbonate.
claims.verbatim:
Barium was isolated as an element in 1774;
however, it was not classed as a metal until 1808.

claims.claim_text: Wallach reports that barium accumulates unevenly across the plant world. Marine plants carry it at around 30 ppm, with the highest levels in brown algae, while typical land plants hold only about 14 ppm. The standout is the fruit of Bertholletia excelea, which he calls a genuine barium concentrator — it can build up to 4,000 ppm, hundreds of times the level of ordinary land plants.
claims.verbatim:
plants at 30 ppm (highest in brown algae); land plants at 14 ppm (the fruit of
Bertholletia excelea is a barium concentrator and can have up to 4,000 ppm);

claims.claim_text: Wallach reports that yttrium does not stay locked in rock but genuinely enters living things. Among plants it accumulates in ferns, and in animals it is found in mammalian bone, teeth and liver. This uptake into living tissue is part of his case that rare earths like yttrium belong in the diet rather than being dismissed as inert geology.

Wallach gives arsenic a colorful word-history. The name was taken from the Syriac word al zarniga and the Persian word Zarnikh, both meaning 'yellow pigment' (a nod to the gold-colored ore orpiment). Rendered into Greek as arsenikos, it carried the sense of 'masculine.' From there it was adopted into Latin as arsenicum and into Old French as arsenic, which is where the English word we use today came from.
claims.verbatim:
The word “arsenic” was taken from the Syriac word al zarniga and the Persian
word Zarnikh, which translates to “yellow pigment," translated into Greek as
arsenikos, and which translates into “masculine.” The word was adopted in Latin
as arsenicum and Old French as arsenic from which the English word “arsenic” was
coined.

claims.claim_text: According to Wallach, arsenic was first isolated and identified in 1250 by Albertus Magnus. The substance itself was known and used far earlier, with a history reaching back to ancient China, the Greeks and the Romans. Separately, he records that the French Academy first identified arsenic in dead human bodies in 1834.
claims.verbatim: Arsenic was first isolated and identified in 1250 by Albertus Magnus

claims.claim_text: Wallach recounts that through the 18th, 19th and 20th centuries a number of arsenic compounds were used as stimulants and medicines. Arsphenamine (developed by Paul Ehrlich) and arsenic trioxide (associated with Thomas Fowler) were among them, and arsphenamine along with neosalvarsan was indicated for syphilis and trypanosomiasis. He adds that arsenic trioxide has been used in various ways for some 500 years, most commonly against cancer, and that the U.S. FDA approved it in 2000 for acute promyelocytic leukemia — with arsenic also used as 'Fowler's solution' for psoriasis.
claims.verbatim:
During the 18th, 19th and 20th centuries, a number of arsenic compounds
were used as stimulants and medicines, including arsphenamine (Paul Ehrlich)
and arsenic trioxide (Thomas Fowler). Arsphenamine as well as neosalvarsan was
indicated for syphilis and trypanosomiasis.

claims.claim_text: Tin, whose chemical symbol is Sn, is a trace mineral that Wallach places among the essential nutrients the body needs. He notes it belongs to the fourth main chemical group of elements, so it shares many chemical and physical properties with carbon, silica, germanium, and lead. Although tin's presence in body tissue was once written off as environmental contamination, Wallach says careful studies later showed it to be a genuine essential trace element.

of elements, Sn has many chemical and physical properties similar to those of
carbon, silica, germanium, and lead.

claims.claim_text: Wallach reports that tin is genuinely present in living tissue, not just in the environment. In land animals it runs about 0.15 ppm, with the highest concentrations found in the lungs and intestines of vertebrates; among plants it is highest in bryophytes (mosses) and lichens. This distribution in living organisms is part of why he treats tin as a real, biologically active trace element rather than a stray contaminant.

claims.claim_text: Wallach links age-related hearing loss in men to tin deficiency. He cites a federal study released in November 1991 which found that men in recent generations have poorer hearing at any given age than men in earlier generations -- a decline he says is generally thought to be the result of tin (Sn) deficiency. He adds that men over the age of 30 lose their hearing more than twice as fast as women of the same age.

claims.claim_text: Wallach describes praseodymium, a 'light' rare earth, as something found throughout the living world, not only in rock. Land plants can accumulate it up to 46 ppm (Carya spp., the hickory tree), and in animals it accumulates in mammalian bone and liver after ingestion. He uses this to make the point that praseodymium enters and builds up in living tissue — part of why he treats it as a plant-derived mineral the body takes in.

In his framework rhenium is treated not as an incidental metal but as one of the plant-derived minerals humans require. He acknowledges that many minerals on the list are not 'classically' considered essential, yet argues each meets two or more of his criteria for an essential nutrient.

claims.claim_text: According to Wallach, thulium is present in living things only in minute traces, about 0.0015 ppm in land plants and just 0.00004 ppm in land animals, far less even than in the rocks it turns up in. It is a 'heavy' rare earth found across igneous rocks, shale, sandstone, and limestone, yet everywhere in scarce quantities. Wallach's broader point is that rare earths like thulium, once carried to us through mineral-rich soils and plants, are now largely absent from the modern food supply.

He notes it occurs naturally at very low concentrations throughout the environment, from igneous rocks and shale down to land plants and living animal tissue. He also lists it among the plant-derived minerals found in high-quality humic shale that a mineral-deficient diet should replace through supplementation.

claims.claim_text: Ytterbium (symbol Yb) is one of the rare-earth elements Wallach catalogues as a naturally occurring trace mineral. He records it thinly scattered through the environment -- roughly 3 ppm in igneous rocks, 1.8 ppm in shale, 1.3 ppm in sandstone and 0.43 ppm in limestone -- and present in living things at far smaller levels, from 0.0015 ppm in land plants down to 0.00012 ppm in land animals. What stands out in his account is that, despite those vanishingly small dietary amounts, ytterbium concentrates once inside the body, building up to as much as 0.3 ppm in bone, teeth and liver.

claims.claim_text: Citrulline is the raw material the body uses to make the amino acid arginine. Wallach's Epigenetics explains that arginine is synthesized from citrulline through two cytosolic enzymes — argininosuccinate synthetase (ASS) and argininosuccinate lyase (ASL). The book notes this conversion is energy-expensive, because producing each molecule of argininosuccinate along the way requires spending ATP (adenosine triphosphate, the cell's energy currency); one reason it gives for supplementing arginine directly is that doing so leaves more ATP available to fuel other cell functions. In short, citrulline sits one step upstream of arginine in the body's biochemistry.

chemist Ernst Schultze and is synthesized from citrulline by the sequential
employment of the cytosolic enzymes argininosuccinate synthetase (ASS) and

argininosuccinate lyase (ASL).

claims.claim_text: Nitric oxide (NO) is a compound the body produces from the amino acid arginine. According to Wallach's Epigenetics, oral arginine supplementation is required for nitric oxide synthesis, and it lowers blood pressure and increases blood flow through obstructed (narrowed or blocked) blood vessels. The same passage also credits oral arginine with reducing healing time after trauma — and being particularly useful for bone trauma — alongside supporting cell division, wound healing, and immune function. In Wallach's framing, nitric oxide is the molecule behind arginine's circulation benefits: easier blood flow and lower blood pressure.
claims.verbatim:
The oral supplementation of
arginine is required for the synthesis of nitric oxide (NO), the reduction of healing
time following trauma, and is particularly useful for bone trauma; it reduces
blood pressure and increases blood flow through obstructed blood vessels.

claims.claim_text: Serotonin is a neurotransmitter — a chemical that carries signals in the nervous system. The body builds it from the essential amino acid tryptophan using the enzyme tryptophan hydroxylase, which is why tryptophan is called serotonin's biochemical precursor. Serotonin can then be converted a step further into the neurohormone melatonin. In the same discussion Wallach notes that conditions cutting tryptophan absorption — fructose malabsorption, lactose intolerance, and gluten intolerance — lower blood tryptophan and are tied to clinical depression, and that a tryptophan metabolite (5-HTP) rapidly crosses into the brain where it is converted to serotonin (also called 5-hydroxytryptamine, or 5-HT).

The book covers melatonin only briefly, within its discussion of tryptophan — an amino acid it notes is sold as a sleep aid — rather than as a standalone topic.

It works in acyl-group activation and transfer reactions — the chemistry that hands molecular fragments from one step to the next — and these reactions are essential for releasing energy from carbohydrates, for gluconeogenesis (making new glucose), for both building up and breaking down fatty acids, and for synthesizing important compounds including sterols, steroid hormones, porphyrins, and the neurotransmitter acetylcholine.

in acylation reactions.

claims.claim_text: Acetylcholine is one of the body's most common neurotransmitters — a chemical messenger that carries a signal across the gap between nerve cells. It works by binding to receptors on the receiving cell and altering that membrane's permeability to specific ions, which either fires the cell (depolarizing it) or quiets it (hyperpolarizing it). The body assembles acetylcholine in the central nervous system, drawing on choline as a structural component, and its production also relies on the acyl-transfer reactions run by coenzyme A, the active form of vitamin B5.

claims.claim_text: Gamma-linolenic acid (GLA) is an omega-6 fatty acid that Wallach places in the "conditionally essential" group of fats — fatty acids the body can normally make on its own but that must come from the diet under certain conditions. This sets it apart from the two fatty acids he calls strictly essential (alpha-linolenic acid, an omega-3, and linoleic acid, an omega-6). Alongside GLA, the conditionally essential group includes arachidonic acid (an omega-6) and docosahexaenoic acid or DHA (an omega-3).

claims.claim_text: DHA (docosahexaenoic acid) is an omega-3 fatty acid. Wallach explains that DHA together with EPA (eicosapentaenoic acid) is required for the enzyme pathways the body uses to process long-chain polyunsaturated fats. He ties DHA directly to mental health: a low level of DHA in the blood is a marker for low brain levels of 5-HIAA (a serotonin breakdown product), and low brain 5-HIAA is directly associated with higher rates of depression and suicide. Elsewhere he places DHA in the "conditionally essential" group of fats and lists DHA and EPA among the nutrients that support memory and cognition.

Low brain concentrations of 5-HIAA is directly associated with increased rates of

claims.claim_text: Arsenic trioxide — the arsenic compound that 18th-century physician Thomas Fowler turned into a medicine — has been used medicinally for roughly 500 years, most often against cancer. In 2000 the U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved it to treat acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL), an often-fatal cancer of the blood and bone marrow. A 1998 New England Journal of Medicine report from Memorial Sloan-Kettering researchers found that low doses of arsenic trioxide destroyed the cancerous cells in 12 seriously ill APL patients and brought them into remission; Chinese researchers had reported the same result in 1997 (journal Blood), and their survivors were still leukemia-free ten years later. Arsenic is also used, as "Fowler's solution," to treat psoriasis.
claims.verbatim:
The doctors were the first in Western medicine to show that low
doses of arsenic trioxide are effective in destroying such cancerous cells.

claims.claim_text: Wallach labels Korsakoff's syndrome 'cerebral beriberi' — beriberi being the classic thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency disease, here affecting the brain. He places it in a family of brain-lesion diseases — multiple sclerosis, ALS (Lou Gehrig's disease), Alzheimer's, Wernicke-Korsakoff's (which he calls 'cerebral beriberi and multiple sclerosis combined'), and Creutzfeld-Jakob disease (mad cow disease) — that he says all share a broad symptom list and brain-lesion pattern with Huntington's disease. The label reinforces his central claim that this 'dementia' is a reversible nutrient-deficiency problem, not permanent damage.
